'''Letícia Parente '''  (1930–1991)  was a [[Brazilians|Brazilian]] visual artist who specialized in politically charged [[video art]].<ref name="Jaqueline">{{ citation | url= http://galeriajaquelinemartins.com.br/artista/leticia-parente | title= Leticia Parente | website=Galeria jacqueline Martins}}</ref> Her surreal short films feature elements of [[body art]] and [[performance art]]. Much of her work is centered around protesting the use of mass [[torture]] by the [[military dictatorship in Brazil]] throughout the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shtromberg |first=Elena |title=Art systems : Brazil and the 1970s |date=2016 |isbn=978-1-4773-0808-0 |edition=First edition, 2016 |location=Austin |oclc=931538928}}</ref> Besides her work in activism and art, Parente also held a [[PhD]] in [[chemistry]] and never left her scientific career after discovering art.<ref name="Hammer">{{ citation | url= https://hammer.ucla.edu/radical-women/artists/leticia-parente/ | website= Hammer.UCLA| title= Leticia Parente }}</ref>

== Biography ==

Letícia Parente was born in [[Salvador, Bahia|Salvador, Bahia, Brazil]] in 1930. While originally pursuing a degree in chemistry, she became interested in art at the age of 41 and studied printing techniques at the Núcleo de Artes e Criatividade in [[Rio de Janeiro]]. Shortly after, she met other artists like [[Anna Bella Geiger]] and [[Sonia Andrade]] who introduced her to video art.<ref name="Images of Torture" /> Besides video art, Parente and her artist peers were also pioneers of other experimental art forms in Brazil during the 1970s. These included works of experimental audio-visual slides, photography, mail art, and utilization of [[Xerox|xeroxing]]. The slideshow was an especially popular medium among Brazilian artists in the 1970's.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Gaviria |first=Paulina Pardo |date=2021-03-31 |title=Letícia Parente's Video In (1975) in Context |url=https://post.moma.org/leticia-parentes-video-in-1975-in-context/ |access-date=2022-04-12 |website=post |publisher=Museum of Modern Art |language=en-US}}</ref> Parente notably used this medium in her piece ''Auto-retrato'' (1975), a compilation of twenty-eight slides of photographs depicting a variety of subjects ranging from objects to people.<ref name=":0" /> Unfortunately, due to the fragile nature of the materials used by Parente to create her works and lack of means of preservation through proper art institutions, most of her 1970s projects have been lost to time.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Parente |first=Letícia |title=Letícia Parente : arqueologia do cotidiano : objetos de uso |date=2011 |others=André Parente, Katia Maciel, Oi Futuro, Museu de Arte Moderna da Bahia, Museu de Arte Contemporânea |isbn=978-85-64140-01-1 |edition=1a edição |location=Rio de Janeiro |oclc=865021756}}</ref>

Alongside her discovery and love for art, Parente also continued to pursue her career in science. She completed her master's degree at [[Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro|Pontifícia Universidade Católica]] in analytical chemistry in 1972, and obtained her Livre Docente title in inorganic chemistry in 1976 through the [[Fluminense Federal University|Universidade Federal Fluminense]]. She would go on to teach chemistry in higher-education institutions in both Brazil and Italy, and also published a handful of books and articles based on her studies.<ref name="Hammer" /> 

== Art ==

Throughout her life, Parente created sixteen films. Four were lost somewhere along the line, likely in a fire or thrown away. <ref name="Another Screen">{{Cite web |url=https://www.another-screen.com/seis-vezes-mulher |title= Six Times Woman |date= 2025 |first=Patricia |last=Andrade }}</ref> Her most well known work is ''Marca Registrada'', or "Trademark", a silent [[VHS]] film which depicts the artist sewing the words "MADE IN BRASIL" onto the sole of her foot.<ref name="Images of Torture">{{ citation | url= https://hammer.ucla.edu/blog/2017/11/images-of-torture-in-videos-by-leticia-parente-in-radical-women/ | title= Images of Torture in Videos by Leticia Parente in Radical Women | date= November 21, 2017 | first=Myriam | last=Gurba }}</ref> Another film from the same period, ''In'', follows Parente as she suspends herself using a dresser hanger in a closet. According to artist [[Myriam Gurba]], this video serves in part as an allusion to the execution of Brazilian journalist [[Vladimir Herzog]] by torture. The police attempted to [[cover-up]] his death as a [[suicide]] and he was found hanged in his prison cell.<ref name="Images of Torture" /> Her film, ''Preparação I'' from 1975 is a political commentary on female [[beauty standards]] of the era. It shows Parente placing [[bandages]] over her face and drawing the appropriate features on top of them. A secondary film was created in 1976, ''Preparação II.'' It depicts Parente injecting herself four times over with different socio-political messaged vaccines. (Ex. anti-colonialism, anti-racism, etc.)  

In 1976, Parente combined her dual interests in science and art to create the exhibition ''Medidas'' (Measurements), held at the [[Museum of Modern Art, Rio de Janeiro]]. Visitors used scientific and pseudoscientific devices to measure their own physical, intellectual, and emotional conditions, for the purpose of "...exposing both the power and the limitations of [[scientific method]]s to assess, classify, and regulate individuals' bodies and subjectivities."<ref name="Hammer" /> This exhibition is considered to be the first exhibition in Brazil to combine science and art.<ref name="Hammer" />

== Themes ==

Similar themes appear in all of Parente's works. She primarily conveys Brazilian socio-political statements in an absurd and experimental manner. Focusing mainly on feminist themes, such as women's [[docile]] environments. Her act of applying makeup, as seen in ''Preparation I'', examines how women transform their faces into an image with no agency.<ref name="Another Screen" /> ''Task 1'' displays Parente's clothes being ironed while she is still wearing them. This illustrates how often society overlooks women and the work they do.<ref name="Another Screen" /> She experiments with the human body to explain her views in a jarring way until it is disfigured and exploited. Treating the body as a stage to perform on.<ref name="Another Screen" />

== Career ==

Parente began teaching chemistry in 1950 at the Federal University of Ceará and Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro.<ref name="Shiva Gallery">{{Cite web |title=Letícia Parente (Salvador, 1930- Rio de Janeiro, 1991). |url=https://shivagallery.org/leticia-parente |publisher=John Jay College |language=en-US}}</ref> She published her first [[monograph]], "Electronegativity," in 1969 and was awarded the Oto de Alencar Award in 1970.<ref name="Letícia Parente">{{Cite web |title=Letícia Parente |url=https://www.leticiaparente.art/biografia?lang=en |publisher=etícia Parente Biografia |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1972, she went to the Center for Art and Creativity to study. In 1976, she taught [[Inorganic Chemistry]] using the process of free teaching.<ref name="Letícia Parente" /> In 1977, she won her position in UFC as Full Professor in the Small Press Festival Competition in [[Antwerp]], [[Belgium]]. This allowed her to implement a postgraduate course on Inorganic Chemistry.<ref name="Letícia Parente" /> In 1984 she got a postdoctoral intership at the [[Université de Nice]], [[France]] for her work in inorganic chemistry. By 1985, she had her second Master's degree in Philosophy of Education from Fundação Getulio Vargas in Italy.<ref name="Letícia Parente" /> In 1987, she helped start Science Education programs at the Science Center in Rio de Janeiro.<ref name="Letícia Parente" />

== Awards and nominations ==

Parente's monograph, "Electronegativity" (1969), won the Oto de Alencar Award in 1970.
